name: Martha of Bethany

seo.title: Saint Martha of Bethany: her life, her faith and her feast day
seo.description: Martha in plain words: the friend who served Jesus while Mary listened, her faith at her brother's tomb, her feast days, and the dragon legend.

band.lede: She welcomed Jesus into her home and worked while her sister listened. When her brother died, she went out to meet Him and called Him the Christ.

picture.alt: A painting by Cornelis Buys: Martha, a young woman with red-gold hair tied up with pink ribbons, sits in a red cloak over a golden gown with pink sleeves. She holds a holy-water sprinkler in her right hand and a golden bucket in her left. At the lower right, the head of a small dragon peers out beside her. Behind her is a blue-green landscape of rocks and towers.

who: Martha lived at Bethany, near Jerusalem, with her sister Mary and her brother Lazarus. Jesus was their friend and their guest. Once, while Mary sat listening at His feet, Martha worked alone and complained. When Lazarus died, she went out to meet Jesus and called Him the Christ, the Son of God. Then He raised her brother.

tidbits.text: John names her first: “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.” He does not even give her sister's name there.
The shortest verse in most English Bibles is in her story. On the way to her brother's tomb, “Jesus wept.”
Tarascon, on the Rhône, still carries a model of the legend's dragon in procession. UNESCO lists it among the giants and dragons of Belgium and France, as living heritage.

cite.text: UNESCO, Processional giants and dragons in Belgium and France

facts.label: In the Bible
facts.text: Only in **Luke** 10 and **John** 11 and 12. Matthew and Mark never name her.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: **Bethany**, a village less than two miles from Jerusalem. Luke says the house was hers. In His last week, Jesus went out to Bethany for the night.

facts.label: Her name
facts.text: Probably Aramaic, meaning **mistress**: the woman in charge of a house. It was in use in her day. A Nabataean inscription dated AD 5, found near Naples, has it.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: Her sister **Mary** and her brother **Lazarus**. Luke never mentions Lazarus. The Bible names no parents, no husband and no children.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Saint Martha**. **Righteous Martha**, in the Orthodox Church, which counts her among the **Myrrh-bearing Women**. The **hostess of our Lord**, in medieval writing.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: The Bible does not say. A medieval legend puts her grave at **Tarascon**, in the south of France, and Rome's 1916 book of martyrs keeps her day there.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Painters often give her the **dragon** of the Tarascon legend, with the **holy water** she threw on it, as at the top of this page. Others paint her busy in the kitchen while Mary listens.

portrait.alt: A Russian icon: Christ in a dark blue robe raises His hand toward Lazarus, who stands wrapped in white at the mouth of a cave cut into steep red and orange rocks. Two women, one in red and one in green, bow at Christ's feet. A young man carries away the stone slab. Apostles stand behind Christ, and a walled city rises at the top.

typeNote: The test names her for that busy day at home, with her sister Mary as her opposite. Martha was busy with all the preparations while Mary sat at Jesus' feet. When their brother died, it was Martha who went out to meet Him.

west.text: **Martha, Mary and Lazarus**, a **Catholic** memorial since 2021. Before that, Rome kept Martha alone. The **Church of England** keeps **Mary, Martha and Lazarus, Companions of Our Lord**. The **Episcopal Church** keeps Mary and Martha of Bethany, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA** keep all three.

east.text: **Righteous Martha and Mary**, the sisters of Lazarus, for the **OCA**. The Orthodox honour them again on the **Sunday of the Myrrh-bearing Women**, two weeks after Pascha.

feasts.note: Why 29 July? The Franciscans put Martha's feast in their calendar in 1262, a week after Mary Magdalene's, and Rome took it up before 1300. For centuries the Latin Church took Martha's sister to be Mary Magdalene, so Martha was kept alone. In 2021 Pope Francis added Mary and Lazarus to her day. Churches on the old calendar keep 4 June 13 days later.

moments.when: On the road with His disciples
moments.title: “Martha, Martha”
moments.text: As Jesus travelled with His disciples, a woman named Martha “welcomed Him into her home.” Her sister Mary sat at the Lord's feet, listening. But Martha “was distracted by all the preparations to be made.” She came and asked Jesus to tell her sister to help her. “Martha, Martha,” the Lord replied, “you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her.”

moments.title: “The one You love is sick”
moments.text: Lazarus, the sisters' brother, fell sick. They sent word to Jesus: “Lord, the one You love is sick.” He answered, “This sickness will not end in death.” John says that Jesus loved all three. Yet on hearing the news, “He stayed where He was for two days.” Then He told His disciples that Lazarus had died, and set out for Judea.

moments.title: She went out to meet Him
moments.text: By the time Jesus came, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. Bethany was “a little less than two miles” from Jerusalem, and many had come out to console the sisters. “So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out to meet Him, but Mary stayed at home.” She told Him her brother would not have died if He had been there. “Your brother will rise again,” Jesus said. Then: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies.” And He asked her, “Do you believe this?” Her answer is below, in her words.

moments.title: “Lazarus, come out!”
moments.text: Martha went back and quietly called Mary, who ran to Jesus and fell at His feet. Seeing her weep, Jesus was deeply moved, and He wept. The tomb was a cave with a stone across the entrance. “Take away the stone,” Jesus said. Martha protested that after four days the body would smell. Jesus replied, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” They took away the stone. Jesus prayed aloud, then called in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” The dead man came out, his hands and feet bound in strips of linen.

moments.title: Martha served
moments.text: Six days before the Passover, Jesus came back to Bethany, and a dinner was given for Him there. “Martha served, and Lazarus was among those reclining at the table with Him.” Mary anointed Jesus' feet with costly perfume and wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with its fragrance. Crowds came to see Lazarus, and the chief priests made plans to kill him too. Here the Bible's story of Martha ends.

words.note: Martha wrote nothing. These are her words as Luke and John record them. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

extras.title: Two sisters, two lives
extras.lede: From early on, Christians read the two sisters as two ways of life: Martha the busy life of serving, Mary the quiet life of prayer. Most ancient writers put Mary's part higher. None of them dismissed Martha's. Here each speaks for himself.

items.title: Augustine: both good
items.text: Both sisters were good, Augustine told his people, and both were loved. “In Martha was the image of things present, in Mary of things to come.” Serving will end in heaven, he says, for no one there will be hungry, or a stranger, or sick. So the Lord “did not blame Martha's work, but distinguished between their services.” Turning to Martha, he says, “You are still on the sea, she is already in port.”
items.quote: You have not chosen a bad part; but she a better.

items.title: Abba Moses: the one thing
items.text: In the Egyptian desert, the monk Abba Moses taught John Cassian that a monk's main aim is to cling to God. He took Martha and Mary as his example. Martha's work was holy: “certainly it was to no unworthy work, but to a praiseworthy service that she summoned her.” But the Lord put first the one thing Mary chose.
items.quote: You see then that the Lord makes the chief good consist in meditation; i.e., in divine contemplation

items.title: Gregory the Great: great, and far better
items.text: Pope Gregory set the sisters beside Jacob's two wives. Leah was fruitful, and Rachel beautiful but barren. So the busy life bears more, he says, and the quiet life sees more. Of Martha and Mary he wrote:
items.quote: Now Martha's concern is not reproved, but that of Mary is even commended. For the merits of the active life are great, but of the contemplative, far better.

cite.text: Gregory the Great, Morals on the Book of Job, Book 6, chapter 37

items.title: John Chrysostom: a time to listen
items.text: Chrysostom was preaching against Christians who used Jesus' words as an excuse to be idle. Paul worked with his hands, he reminded them. What Jesus said to Martha was not about work at all, but about timing:
items.quote: It is our duty to know the right season, and not to spend on carnal things the time proper for listening.

cite.text: John Chrysostom, Homilies on John, Homily 44

items.title: Meister Eckhart: Martha ahead
items.text: Not everyone put Mary first. The medieval German mystic Meister Eckhart argued in a sermon that Martha was the more mature of the two. She no longer depended on religious feelings, and could get on with serving where she was needed. Mary, he thought, would get there too.

cite.text: The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 29 July, on Eckhart's Sermon 86

myths.claim: Jesus told Martha off for working.
myths.truth: He did not tell her to stop. He said she was “worried and upset about many things,” and that Mary had chosen the good portion. The Fathers agreed that her work was not the fault. “Martha's concern is not reproved,” wrote Gregory the Great. Their readings are in Two sisters, two lives, above. At the next supper in Bethany, John says simply, “Martha served.”

cite.text: Luke 10:41-42; John 12:2; Gregory the Great, Morals on the Book of Job, Book 6

myths.claim: Martha's sister Mary was Mary Magdalene.
myths.truth: The Gospels never say so. John's Mary is Martha's sister at Bethany. Mary Magdalene is named for her town, Magdala. For centuries the Latin Church took the two to be one woman, and so Rome kept Martha's day alone. Its 1916 book of martyrs still calls Martha the “sister of blessed Mary Magdalen”. The Orthodox keep them apart: Mary Magdalene on 22 July, Martha and Mary on 4 June. In 2021 Rome added Mary and Lazarus to Martha's day. Its decree said the old uncertainty about Mary had been resolved.

cite.text: John 11:1; the Roman Martyrology (1916), 29 July; Decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship, 26 January 2021

myths.claim: Martha sailed to France and tamed a dragon.
myths.truth: The Bible says nothing of her after the supper at Bethany. The story is in the *Golden Legend*, a book of saints' lives compiled in the 1200s. Martha, Mary, Lazarus and others, it says, were “put into a ship without sail, oars, or rudder” and came to Marseilles. By the Rhône lived a dragon “greater than an ox, longer than an horse”. Martha found it eating a man. “She cast on him holy water, and showed to him the cross,” and bound it with her girdle. The people killed it, and Tarascon took its name from it. The Orthodox tell a different later story: the sisters helped Lazarus preach the Gospel in other lands.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, the Life of S. Martha, tr. William Caxton (1483); OCA, 4 June

circle.name: Mary of Bethany
circle.text: Her sister, who sat at the Lord's feet while Martha served. Before His death she anointed His feet with costly perfume and wiped them with her hair.

circle.name: Lazarus
circle.text: Their brother, whom Jesus called out of the tomb after four days. Afterward the chief priests made plans to kill him too.

circle.name: Jesus
circle.text: Their guest and friend. John says plainly that He loved all three, and He wept on the way to Lazarus's tomb.

saint.big: Yes. The Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches all honour her, most of them together with her sister and brother.
